title: An Overview of the BIOL 4200 Data Science Workflow
text: In BIOL 4200, we will use three main tools to work with data and code:

title: An Overview of the BIOL 4200 Data Science Workflow
text:
How the pieces fit together
Think of the three tools as having different jobs:
GitHub Desktop → Miniconda → VSCode

GitHub Desktop manages your course repository.
Miniconda manages the Python environment used by your course code.
VSCode is where you write and run your code and notebooks.

Your workflow will generally look like this:
               GitHub (Online)
                      ↑
                GitHub Desktop (Syncs files between your local folders and online folders)
                      │
              Your BIOL4200 repository
                      ↓
                   VSCode (For editing code)     Miniconda (makes sure you have the right Python packages)
                      ↓                             ↙
              Jupyter notebooks

title: An Overview of the BIOL 4200 Data Science Workflow
text:
The three tools

GitHub Desktop
What is it?
GitHub Desktop is a graphical interface for Git and GitHub. Git is a version-control system that keeps track of changes to files, while GitHub provides a place to store Git repositories online.
Why do we use it?
For this course, GitHub Desktop gives you an easy way to:

Download your BIOL 4200 repository to your computer.
Save changes to your assignments and lab notebooks.
Synchronize your work with GitHub.
Keep a backup of your work online.
Download updates to course materials.

You do not need to learn Git from the command line to use GitHub Desktop.


Miniconda
What is it?
Miniconda is a lightweight version of Anaconda that provides the Conda package and environment manager. A Conda environment is an isolated collection of Python and other software packages.
Why do we use it?
Python has thousands of packages that can be used for data science. Different packages—and different versions of those packages—can sometimes conflict with one another.
We will create a dedicated environment called biol4200 containing the software needed for this course. This means that everyone can work with a consistent set of tools.


VSCode
What is it?
Visual Studio Code (VSCode) is an integrated development environment (IDE). It allows you to write, edit, and run code in one application. With the Python and Jupyter extensions installed, it can also run Jupyter notebooks.
Why do we use it?
VSCode will be your primary workspace for BIOL 4200. You will use it to:

Open your GitHub repository.
Write and edit Python code.
Run Jupyter notebooks.
View data and plots.
Work with your biol4200 Python environment.

title: An Overview of the BIOL 4200 Data Science Workflow
text:
What you will install
You will need:

GitHub Desktop

VSCode
Python and Jupyter extensions for VSCode

The following pages walk you through installing and configuring each tool.

title: Getting started with Miniconda
text:
Miniconda is a lightweight distribution of Python that includes Conda, a tool for managing Python environments and software packages.
A Conda environment is an isolated installation of Python and the packages needed for a particular project.
Why do we use it in BIOL 4200?
Data science relies on many Python packages, such as NumPy, pandas, matplotlib, and scikit-learn. These packages have dependencies and versions that need to work together.
Rather than installing everything directly into your computer’s main Python installation, we will create a separate environment called:
biol4200
This keeps the BIOL 4200 software separate from other Python projects you may work on.

title: Getting started with Miniconda
text:
Step 1: Install Miniconda
Download Miniconda from:
Download Miniconda
You will need to create a free Anaconda account.
Important: Download Miniconda, not the full Anaconda Distribution.

Mac

Download the Miniconda installer appropriate for your Mac.
Run the installer.
Follow the installation instructions.
If prompted, allow Miniconda to initialize your shell.

After installation, open a new Terminal window.


Windows

Download the Windows Miniconda installer.
Run the installer.
Follow the installation instructions.
Open PowerShell after installation.

Before continuing, Windows may require you to allow locally created scripts to run.
Open PowerShell as Administrator:

Open the Start menu.
Search for PowerShell.
Right-click PowerShell.
Select Run as administrator.
Run:

Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned
If Windows asks you to confirm the change, accept it.
You can then close the Administrator PowerShell window and open a normal PowerShell window.

title: Getting started with Miniconda
text:
Step 2: Open a terminal
You will use the terminal to create and manage your Conda environment.

Mac
Open Terminal.


Windows
Open PowerShell or the terminal provided by your Miniconda installation.
You should be able to run:
conda --version
If Conda was installed correctly, you should see a version number.

title: Getting started with Miniconda
text:
Step 3: Create the BIOL4200 environment
Create a new environment called biol4200 with Python 3.14:
conda create -n biol4200 python=3.14
Conda will ask you to confirm the installation. Type:
y
and press Enter.

title: Getting started with Miniconda
text:
Step 4: Activate the environment
Activate your new environment:
conda activate biol4200
You should now see something like this at the beginning of your command prompt:
(biol4200)
This tells you that you are working inside the BIOL 4200 environment.

Important
You will generally need to activate this environment before running your BIOL 4200 Python code.
If you open a new terminal later, run:
conda activate biol4200
again.

title: Getting started with Miniconda
text:
Step 5: Download the requirements file
Download the BIOL 4200 requirements.txt file from Canvas and place it inside your BIOL4200homework repository.
The file tells Python which packages need to be installed for the course.
Your repository should look something like:
BIOL4200homework/
├── lab_notebook.ipynb
├── requirements.txt
└── ...

title: Getting started with Miniconda
text:
Step 6: Install the required packages
Make sure your biol4200 environment is activated:
conda activate biol4200
Navigate to your repository using the terminal, then run:
pip install -r requirements.txt
This will install the Python packages listed in requirements.txt.

title: Getting started with Miniconda
section: Step 7: Make the environment available to Jupyter
text:
Step 7: Make the environment available to Jupyter
We will use Jupyter notebooks throughout the course.
Install the BIOL 4200 environment as a Jupyter kernel:
python -m ipykernel install --user --name biol4200 --display-name "Python (BIOL4200)"
This tells Jupyter that it can use your biol4200 environment.

title: Getting started with Miniconda
text:
Step 8: Test the installation
Run:
jupyter notebook
If everything was installed correctly, Jupyter should open in your web browser.
You should be able to select:
Python (BIOL4200)
as a notebook kernel.

title: Getting started with Miniconda
text:
Troubleshooting
If conda is not recognized, close your terminal and open a new one.
On Windows, you may need to open the Anaconda Prompt application and run
conda init
If conda activate biol4200 does not work on Windows, open PowerShell in administrator mode and run the following command:
Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned
If you receive an error while installing packages, make sure that your biol4200 environment is activated before running:
pip install -r requirements.txt

title: Getting started with GitHub Desktop
text:
GitHub Desktop is a graphical application for working with Git and GitHub.
Git is a version-control system. It keeps track of changes to your files so that you can save versions of your work and synchronize those changes with a repository stored on GitHub.
Why do we use it in BIOL 4200?
You will use GitHub Desktop to manage your course repository. In particular, it will allow you to:

Download your BIOL 4200 repository to your computer.
Save your work to GitHub.
Download updates to course materials.
Keep a backup of your work.
Work with Git without using the command line.

title: Getting started with GitHub Desktop

If you do not already have one, create a free GitHub account:
Create a GitHub account

title: Getting started with GitHub Desktop
text:
Step 2: Install GitHub Desktop
Download GitHub Desktop:
Download GitHub Desktop

Mac

Download the macOS version.

Windows

Run the installer.
Open GitHub Desktop.

title: Getting started with GitHub Desktop
text:
Step 3: Create your BIOL4200 repository
On GitHub (online), create a new repository called:
BIOL4200homework
You can make the repository private unless I tell you otherwise.

title: Getting started with GitHub Desktop
text:
Step 4: Clone your repository
Once your repository exists on GitHub:

Open GitHub Desktop.
Select File → Clone repository.
Find your BIOL4200homework repository.
Choose where you would like to store it on your computer. (I recommend Documents/GitHub)
Click Clone.

GitHub Desktop will now create a copy of your repository on your computer. This local copy is the folder that you will open in VSCode.

title: Getting started with GitHub Desktop
text:
Step 5: Add your lab notebook
Place your lab notebook in your BIOL4200homework folder.
You should eventually have something like:
BIOL4200homework/
├── lab_notebook.ipynb
├── requirements.txt
└── ...
The exact contents of the repository will depend on the assignment.

title: Getting started with GitHub Desktop
section: A note about saving your work
text:
A note about saving your work
GitHub Desktop uses a workflow called commit → push.
When you make changes to your files:

GitHub Desktop notices the changes.
You create a commit, which records a snapshot of your changes.
You push the commit to GitHub.

You should get into the habit of committing and pushing your work regularly. That way, if something goes wrong on your computer, your work is safely stored on GitHub.

title: Getting started with VSCode
text:
Visual Studio Code (VSCode) is an integrated development environment (IDE). An IDE is an application that provides tools for writing, editing, and running computer code.
VSCode can also work with Jupyter notebooks, which allow you to combine code, data, visualizations, and written explanations in the same document.
Why do we use it in BIOL 4200?
VSCode will be your primary workspace for the course. You will use it to:

Open your BIOL4200homework repository.
Edit Python code.
Work with Jupyter notebooks.
Run analyses.
Create figures and visualizations.
Select and use your biol4200 Conda environment.

title: Getting started with VSCode
text:
Step 4: Open your BIOL4200 repository

title: Getting started with VSCode
section: Step 5: Select the BIOL4200 Python environment
text:
Step 5: Select the BIOL4200 Python environment
Open your Jupyter notebook.
Near the top-right of the notebook, you should see an option for selecting the kernel.
Click it and select:
Python (BIOL4200)
If you do not see it, you may need to select:
Select Another Kernel → Python Environments
and then choose the Python installation associated with:
biol4200

title: Getting started with VSCode
text:
Step 6: Run a test
Create a new cell in your notebook and enter:
print("Hello, BIOL 4200!")
Run the cell.
You should see:
Hello, BIOL 4200!
You can also test that you are using the correct Python environment:
import sys

print(sys.executable)
The resulting path should contain something indicating that you are using the biol4200 environment.

title: Getting started with VSCode
text:
Your BIOL4200 workflow
Once everything is installed, your typical workflow will look like this:

1. Open GitHub Desktop
Use GitHub Desktop to synchronize your repository with GitHub.


2. Open VSCode
Open your BIOL4200homework folder.


3. Select the BIOL4200 environment
Make sure your notebook is using:
Python (BIOL4200)


4. Work on your notebook
Write and run your Python code in VSCode.


5. Save your work
Save your notebook and any other files you have changed.


6. Commit and push your changes
Open GitHub Desktop and commit your changes.
Then push them to GitHub.
This gives you a complete workflow:
GitHub Desktop
      ↓
Download/synchronize your repository
      ↓
     VSCode
      ↓
Write and run your analysis
      ↓
   Miniconda
      ↓
Python + data science packages
      ↓
     VSCode
      ↓
Save your work
      ↓
GitHub Desktop
      ↓
Commit + push
      ↓
    GitHub

title: Getting started with VSCode
text:
Final checklist
Before starting your first assignment, make sure you have:

A GitHub account
A BIOL4200homework repository
GitHub Desktop installed
Your repository cloned to your computer
Miniconda installed
A Conda environment called biol4200
Python 3.14 installed in the environment
requirements.txt in your repository
All required packages installed
A Jupyter kernel called Python (BIOL4200)
VSCode installed
The Python VSCode extension installed
The Jupyter VSCode extension installed
Your BIOL 4200 notebook running successfully

If all of these boxes are checked, you’re ready to start coding!
